subject: Ingress conduit analysis — least-privilege reach for on-prem LLMs
messages:

Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.com

Subject: Ingress options for our private deploy (high-level ask)

Hannah —

Thanks for the call earlier. We need a short write-up of the connectivity options so our security team can sign off: specifically, whether we should push for VPC peering, PrivateLink-style interface endpoints, or a site-to-site VPN to reach Redwood-hosted inference from our on-prem datacenter. Key constraints:

- Least-privilege access (zero standing broad network routes)
- Auditability and token scoping for model calls
- Minimal blast radius in case of a compromise
- Reasonable latency for inference (95th percentile under 120ms for short prompts)

Can you outline trade-offs and a recommended default plus a dev/test fallback? Also include any artifacts we should hand to our network ops people.

Appreciate it,
Olivia
Director, Platform Security
Century Health

From: hannah_schmitt@redwood.com
To: Olivia Nguyen <olivia@centuryhealth.com>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.com, jordan_blake@redwood.com
Date: 2026-08-25T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Ingress options for our private deploy (high-level ask)

Olivia —

Thanks, this is exactly the prompt we wanted. I pulled Jordan and Kim in for the infra tradeoffs. High level summary attached (ingress-options-summary.pdf).

Quick bullets so your security team has immediate answers:
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): strongest network-level least-privilege boundary. No cross-VPC routing required. Allows per-endpoint IAM + token scoping.
- S2S VPN (IPsec): flexible, broadly supported, good for dev and legacy systems but opens a routed path between networks (larger blast radius) and weaker identity granularity unless combined with proxy auth.
- VPC peering: high-throughput, simple, but symmetric routing and no native endpoint isolation; not recommended if you need strict least-privilege between customer and Redwood environments.

We recommend: Default = PrivateLink for production; S2S VPN for dev/ingress-burst/legacy integrations; avoid peering unless the customer strictly controls network ACLs and accepts the risk.

Jordan will follow with latency/cost tradeoffs and an ops checklist. If you want, we can schedule a 30m network ops + security sync.

Best,
Hannah Schmitt
Senior Solutions Architect — Redwood Inference

From: jordan_blake@redwood.com
To: hannah_schmitt@redwood.com, kimberly_park@redwood.com
Date: 2026-08-26T11:38:00-07:00
Subject: Technical notes: latency and operational tradeoffs (internal)

Hannah / Kim —

Putting numbers on the table for the three patterns. See attached sample measurements (latency-metrics.csv) from a staging run that proxied traffic via our us-west-2 region. Top-level: measured p50/p95 token RTT for a 32-token prompt on a small model and a 512-token context on a medium model. Numbers are sample-based but directional.

PrivateLink
- p50: ~18ms; p95: ~45ms (additional TLS + LB hop)
- Pros: no routable cross-VPC; endpoint-level security; per-endpoint security groups; easier to ACL to specific subnets/IPs
- Cons: small additional egress cost (interface endpoint data processing), more complex initial setup (endpoint service + acceptance), not available cross-cloud if they have multi-cloud on-prem connectors

S2S VPN
- p50: ~34ms; p95: ~120–180ms depending on on-prem gateway and transient congestion
- Pros: quick to provision for PoC; supports encrypted IPSec tunnels to their firewall; vendor-agnostic
- Cons: requires managing tunnel failovers, less identity-level granularity, creates broad routed adjacency unless restricted by on-prem ACL/NAT

VPC Peering
- p50: ~12ms; p95: ~30ms (lowest latency if both VPCs in same region)
- Pros: minimal overhead, good throughput
- Cons: symmetric routing, no service-level endpoint controls, risk of lateral movement if either side is compromised

Operational checklist to hand to customer (short):
- For PrivateLink: provide the endpoint service name, required SGs/ports (443), verification DNS CNAMEs, and expected IP ranges for our egress NVA. Recommend short-lived tokens + mTLS if they want double-auth.
- For S2S VPN: expected peer IPs, pre-shared key handling, IKEv2 profile, BGP vs static routes, MTU guidance, keepalive settings.
- For Peering: VPC IDs/cidr blocks, route-table changes, DHCP/options for DNS resolution, peering acceptance steps and IAM perms list.

I'll add a small script snippet to the shared drive that generates the minimal network ACLs and SG rules for the PrivateLink pattern.

—Jordan
Principal Network Engineer — Redwood Inference

Attachment: latency-metrics.csv (sample measurements)

From: hannah_schmitt@redwood.com
To: Marcus Ruiz <m.ruiz@centuryhealth.com>, Olivia Nguyen <olivia@centuryhealth.com>
Cc: jordan_blake@redwood.com, kimberly_park@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Ingress options for our private deploy (high-level ask) — recommendation and next steps

Marcus / Olivia —

Thanks for the diagram — helpful. Short answers first, then recommended plan and handoff artifacts.

Q1 (firewall rules): you should absolutely keep stateful firewall controls on your on-prem gateway. PrivateLink removes the need for broad VPC routes but does not replace your perimeter controls. Treat the interface endpoint as a single, tightly-scoped destination: allow egress from the application subnets to the endpoint IPs over 443, and keep standard IDS/NSM monitoring in place on the gateway. We recommend short-lived mTLS on top of TLS for high-sensitivity workflows to give you cryptographic identity beyond network-level controls.

Q2 (throughput): PrivateLink scales well for most interactive workloads. For sustained high-throughput batch jobs (large parallel inference), we recommend one of two approaches:
- run batch workloads through a dedicated S2S VPN with a dedicated pipeline and rate-limited egress; or
- use a peered VPC for a dedicated batch path (only if you can accept symmetric routing and ensure strict ACLs).

Recommendation (production): PrivateLink as the primary ingress for model-serving; enforce short-lived tokens + optional mTLS; provide the PrivateLink DNS and SG/IP list (we'll send exact values). This gives the best balance of least-privilege + auditability.

Fallback for dev/batch: S2S VPN for ad-hoc dev and controlled batch lanes. Peering: only for customers who need the absolute lowest latency and can accept the lateral movement risk — we consider peering a last-resort pattern and will require a joint runbook and a quarterly security sweep if used.

Next steps / deliverables (we can prepare these later today):
- PrivateLink configuration sheet (endpoint service name, SG rules, DNS mappings) — redwood/app DR-8743
- S2S VPN runbook with IKEv2 profile and BGP example — attachment to follow if you pick VPN
- Short script that produces minimal SG/ACL entries for your firewall team (we'll put in the shared drive)

If you want, schedule 30 minutes this week for ops and we can walk your network team through the PrivateLink acceptance flow.

Thanks —
Hannah
